analysis.one_liner: Guarantees health coverage for every American through regional alliances, with employer-paid premiums and capped premium growth.
analysis.headline: The Health Security Act, introduced by Senator Moynihan in November 1993 with zero cosponsors, was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar but never got a committee hearing, a floor vote, or a single action after that, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have guaranteed comprehensive health coverage to every legal U.S. resident through regional "health alliances" that pool individuals and employers and negotiate with certified health plans. It required employers to pay part of the premium, capped how fast premiums could grow, barred plans from denying coverage for preexisting conditions, and added a Medicare prescription drug benefit and home-and-community long-term care. It would have been financed partly by higher tobacco taxes, employer assessments, and limits on high-income health subsidies.
analysis.who_benefits: The uninsured, who would get guaranteed comprehensive coverage including prescription drugs, dental, vision, and mental health services; people with preexisting conditions, whom plans could no longer reject, price by health status, or drop; workers who change or lose jobs, whose coverage would follow them; low-income families, who get reduced cost sharing and premiums; and Medicare beneficiaries, who would gain an outpatient prescription drug benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible resident is entitled to a comprehensive benefit package covering hospital care, prescription drugs, preventive services, mental health and substance abuse treatment, dental and vision care, and more [S2][S3].

Health plans are barred from refusing enrollees for preexisting conditions, imposing waiting periods, excluding individuals with riders, or discriminating by health status, age, disability, or income [S2].
Annual out-of-pocket costs are capped at $1,500 per individual and $3,000 per family, with reduced cost sharing and premium discounts for low-income families [S2].

Medicare beneficiaries would gain coverage of outpatient prescription drugs, with manufacturer rebates to the government, and a new federal program would fund home and community-based services for people with disabilities [S2].
The bill repeals the insurance industry's antitrust exemption for health benefits under the McCarran-Ferguson Act and toughens fraud-and-abuse penalties [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who must make premium payments scaled to their size and average wages plus assessments on corporate alliances and retiree health costs; smokers and tobacco companies, through higher excise taxes; high-income individuals, whose health care subsidies are recaptured and whose S-corporation and partnership income becomes subject to self-employment tax; and taxpayers, who fund the federal alliance payments, Medicare drug benefit, and public health programs. Individuals must also enroll in a plan and pay any required premium.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, tobacco buyers, and high earners

drawbacks.text: The bill requires every eligible individual to enroll in a health plan and pay the required premium, a mandate with real costs for households that previously went uncovered by choice [S2].

Mandatory employer premiums and assessments raise labor costs, a burden small businesses warned would fall on wages and hiring; the bill's employer premium formula does vary with firm size and average wages [S2].

A new National Health Board of seven presidential appointees gets sweeping authority over benefits, premiums, cost containment, and health information systems, concentrating major regulatory power in one executive-branch body [S2].

Premium caps and bid limits could pressure plans and providers' revenues; the bill cuts Medicare hospital and physician payment updates and freezes skilled nursing updates to help pay for the expansion [S2].
Medical malpractice lawsuits are barred until mandatory alternative dispute resolution concludes, and plaintiffs must file a specialist's affidavit, limiting ordinary patients' legal recourse [S2].
Higher tobacco taxes are regressive, falling hardest on lower-income smokers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside was the largest proposed expansion of guaranteed health coverage in American history: universal comprehensive benefits, portability, an end to preexisting-condition denials, and out-of-pocket caps, paid for substantially by employers, tobacco taxes, and high-income households. The costs were real and serious: mandatory premiums and a new federal regulatory apparatus with broad price-setting power, spending cuts in Medicare to help finance it, and restrictions on malpractice suits. Whether premium caps could hold costs down without degrading quality was the strongest good-faith objection, and the bill's sheer complexity (eleven titles covering alliances, boards, financing, workers' compensation, and auto insurance coordination) made implementation a genuine gamble.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee ever considered it, no vote was ever scheduled, and it expired when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan introduced the Health Security Act in the Senate on November 22, 1993 [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point [S4].
It was read a second time on November 23, 1993 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 339 [S5].
That was the last action of any kind: the bill never received a committee referral, hearing, markup, or floor vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers were better off because no mandatory employer premium or assessment was ever enacted, and the health insurance industry kept its existing business model without community-rating mandates, premium caps, or the loss of its antitrust exemption. Americans without coverage gained nothing from this bill's failure, though the broader 103rd Congress fight over health reform ended without any major overhaul.

for.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Health Security Act in the Senate on November 22, 1993; the bill was read twice and placed on the calendar, with no further action

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Proposed the Health Security Act plan to Congress in 1993 and publicly campaigned for universal coverage legislation; this Senate bill carried his framework

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate Minority Leader and Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Clinton health plan and blocked any path to a floor vote; no Republican supported this bill and it never came to the floor

against.name: Health Insurance Association of America
against.what_they_did: Funded the 'Harry and Louise' advertising campaign against the Clinton plan's mandated coverage and alliance structure

against.name: Sen. George Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled this bill for floor action; in 1994 he instead brought a narrower substitute health bill that failed a procedural vote needing 60 senators

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls were ever taken on this bill, but the surrounding health reform fight split by party: the plan came from a Democratic president with a Democratic Senate sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, while Senate Republicans opposed it.

industries.note: The bill would have regulated insurers heavily, forcing guaranteed issue, community rating, and premium caps while eliminating their antitrust exemption, but it also made private health plans the permanent channel for universal coverage, delivering them tens of millions of mandated customers through the alliances. The industry publicly opposed the bill and kept its existing business model when it died.

Employers would owe premium payments scaled to size and wages, plus assessments on large corporate alliances and retiree health costs, and would face reporting, auditing, and anti-discrimination rules. Many employees would have gained coverage their employers did not previously fund.

Higher excise taxes on cigarettes and other tobacco products, plus a new tax on roll-your-own tobacco, would directly raise their products' cost to fund coverage. Their interest in avoiding the tax ran against the public financing of coverage.

Providers would gain guaranteed payment for all patients and new funding for academic health centers, graduate medical education, and community clinics, but would face Medicare payment cuts, premium caps, and tighter fraud and self-referral enforcement.

A new Medicare outpatient drug benefit and expanded drug coverage would enlarge their market, but manufacturer rebates to the government and an advisory review of breakthrough-drug launch prices would cut into pricing power.
